News.title: Horrifying moment girl, 16, plunges to her death from cliff swing after ‘shouting her safety rope wasn’t tight enough’
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a teenage girl tragically died after plunging from a cliff swing in China.

Just moments before the girl fell, she reportedly shouted that her safety rope had not been done up tight enough.





Terrifying footage of the horrific accident was caught by her friend at the Maliuyan Waterfall scenic spot in the city of Huaying on Sunday.

The 16-year-old, identified only by her surname Liu, was seen holding a flag, eagerly waiting for her flight across the lookout.

Smiling just seconds before her fatal plunge, Liu was strapped into the harness as staff prepared to send her out over the gorge.

In the background of the video, her friends could be heard excitedly chattering as she moved towards the edge of the platform.



According to local media, Liu could then be heard shouting several times that the rope was “not tight enough” before she was launched from the secure area.

In just seconds, tragedy struck, as Liu plunged over the drop and slipped down a few inches as the rope came loose.



One of the attendants on the platform reached towards her, but she was already too far gone, plummeting into the valley.

Local media outlets reported the safety rope snapped as soon as she left the platform, sending her falling onto the rocks below.

Emergency services rushed to the scene, but Liu sadly died on the way to hospital.

The cliff swing was reportedly being operated by an outdoor adventure company known as Chongqing Adventure Camp.

The company had promoted the attraction on its WeChat public account in March.



Officials have since closed the scenic area.

An investigation has since been launched into the deadly incident.

Local authorities have classified the incident as a production safety responsibility accident following their preliminary inquiries.

The park has also announced it would remain shut between May 4 and May 10.

A maintenance check for the equipment is also being undertaken.



One of the staff members for the operator said the company was in contact with Liu’s family and had been cooperating with authorities.

The shocking accident has sparked a conversation on Chinese social media platform Weibo.

Users have slammed operators for allegedly ignoring Liu’s warnings.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

One user even said the company had “disregarded human life”.

“A small oversight has taken away the future of this young girl,” they wrote.

News.title: ‘Incel’ ex-Army cadet, 17, locked up for plotting horrific mass shooting at his school prom after girl rejected him
News.content:
TERROR TEEN ‘Incel’ ex-Army cadet, 17, locked up for plotting horrific mass shooting at his school prom after girl rejected him

A FORMER Army cadet has been locked up after plotting a horrific mass shooting at his school prom after a girl rejected him.

Dihan Rahman, now aged 19, made a Nazi salute and held a rope noose in selfies and posted the personal details of two girls and a teacher during an online stalking campaign.





On Wednesday, the teenager was sentenced at the Old Bailey to four-and-a half-years in prison with an extended licence period of three years.

Previously, the court heard how problems began in 2023 after Rahman attended a new school and an Army cadet programme.

When one of the girls rejected Rahman’s advances, he began sending them both abusive messages, jurors were told.

One of the girls became aware that he was taking pictures of her and her female friends and he began “spamming” her social media accounts.

After he was banned from the cadet base, Rahman posted on Snapchat and TikTok that he planned to “ruin prom”, forcing organisers to change the venue twice.

Rahman’s friendship with the second girl was said to have deteriorated in early 2024 when he criticised her weight on Snapchat.



The girl, who was involved in organising the prom, told an adult and Rahman was given a two-day school suspension, the court was told.

The female teacher said she had no problems with him until he started sending the two girls Snapchat messages in January 2024.

The teacher seized his phone after he was reported for taking photographs of girls at school.

She saw a photograph of the defendant in cadet uniform holding a noose and caught him deleting images after she briefly left the room.

As she confiscated the device, she viewed a picture of Rahman with a headscarf around his face with an image saying “Who’s in for a Valentines school shooting”.



Another picture showed Rahman in Army uniform with the words “kill yourself”, images of Adolf Hitler, Saddam Hussein, beheadings and dead bodies, as well as depictions of violence against women.

Jurors were shown pictures of Rahman in military fatigues, giving a Nazi salute and holding a green cord tied in a noose.

He was arrested at his home on March 15, 2024 and given police bail on condition he stay away from the girls, which he failed to do.

In November 2025, Rahman was arrested again and an examination of his laptop revealed he had made 83 searches for the first girl that month – he was remanded in custody.

Further investigations revealed that documents about both girls had been released online with details about their family and social media accounts and saying they were a “danger to males”, jurors were told.



Prosecutor Serena Gates KC told jurors this was “doxxing” – an online practice of exposing personal information about others to encourage online trolls to harass them.

She went on to describe how Rahman had made official complaints against the teacher, pretending to be his own father.

Rahman had initially denied having documents useful for terrorism, claiming he had them for “research”.

Ms Gates said the defendant’s electronic devices and notes revealed a “mixed” ideology touching on the extreme right-wing, Islamic State, Incel and hatred of women.

She told the court: “The common ground is the hatred of Jews and there is also material on how women are treated within those ideologies.”



Rahman had also been a “trusted” administrator of an extreme right-wing network on Telegram having pretended to be a white youth, the court heard.

He pleaded guilty to three counts of stalking and three counts of possession of indecent images.

On the second day of his trial, Rahman, from west London, admitted three charges of possessing documents useful for terrorism.

They included a pipebomb tutorial and a video on how to make TATP explosives.

On Wednesday, Judge Simon Mayo KC sentenced him at the Old Bailey to four-and-a half-years in prison with an extended licence period of three years.



He told Rahman: “This is not a case of a single lapse or a moment of poor judgment.

“Much of the behaviour was planned, concealed, and persistent. It occurred over a prolonged period and, significantly, it continued even after the police became involved and you were subject to bail conditions.”

His stalking, which included making malicious professional complaints against the teacher, was “persistent, calculated and highly intrusive”, he said.

Judge Mayo added: “The impact of your stalking was severe and enduring. The two young women lived in constant fear, altered daily routines, withdrew socially and restricted online activity.

“Their education suffered, a school prom was relocated twice with additional security, and one of the young women ultimately changed colleges. Both continue to experience anxiety and loss of confidence.



“No sentence I can pass will remove the anxiety, fear, and psychological harm which you caused your victims.”

The judge noted the defendant’s autism spectrum disorder, emotional immaturity and social isolation, but said none of these factors excused his behaviour.

The two girls Rahman stalked attended his sentencing and made victim impact statements from behind a screen in court with one saying she is now “cautious about the friends I have” and used to have a “large social circle”.

Bethan David, head of counter terrorism for the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “Today’s sentencing reflects the seriousness of his crimes, and I hope can bring some closure to his victims, my thoughts remain with them.”

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: “This case is yet another example of a growing and concerning trend of young people being drawn into extremist, violent and terrorist ideologies – principally from what they are exposed to and consuming online.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Rahman’s actions towards his victims – two of whom were teenage girls – were completely unacceptable and I want to praise their incredible courage and resilience throughout this whole ordeal.

“I would also like to praise the actions of Rahman’s teachers who contacted police with their concerns, which enabled us to intervene and investigate when we did.”

News.title: Moment teacher ‘who sexually abused and murdered adopted baby’ wails ‘it’s my fault’ after being told he won’t survive
News.content:
THIS is the moment a teacher accused of sexually assaulting and murdering a baby he was adopting wailed “it’s my fault” to nurses, a court heard.

Footage shows Jamie Varley collapse crying to the ground after being told Preston Davey would not survive.





Varley, 36, had allegedly sexually assaulted the 13-month-old then smothered him – causing the tot to go into cardiac arrest.

He and boyfriend John McGowan-Fazakerley are currently on trial at Preston Crown Court.

Jurors were today shown the video of Varley wearing a red Jurassic Park T-shirt and tartan pyjama bottoms while sobbing in the hospital.

He pleaded with hospital doctors to “kill me” and wailed loudly: “It’s all my fault”.

Nurses and police could be seen trying to comfort Varley as he cries “I can’t, no, I have done this”.

When of the hospital staff tells him that Preston needs him, he replies: “He doesn’t need me, it’s my fault…please get my mum…this is not happening…please kill me, please kill me.”



The court heard when Varley eventually went to see and cradle dead son, he was heard saying: “I probably won’t see you again, I’m definitely going to hell.”

Varley was described as “hysterical” and told doctors he had left the baby in the bath while he had a shower and returned three to four minutes later.

But Dr Wendy Aubrey, a senior anaesthetist, told the jury there was no water in Preston’s lungs despite Varley’s claims about the bath.



Medics worked for nearly an hour to resuscitate the baby on July 27, 2023, until a decision was made that further intervention was futile.

Jurors heard Varley then tried to give chest compressions and mouth to mouth resuscitation to Preston, despite the breathing tube being still in place.

Dr Aubrey added: “I had to be really quite firm and tell him to stop because of what he was continuing trying to do to Preston.”

Varley and McGowan-Fazakerley both deny sexually assaulting Preston, who they were in the process of formally adopting.

The court heard Preston began living with the couple in their Blackpool home in April 2023 after undergoing an assessment and familiarisation process.



But just days later Varley, who took a year off work as head of year at a high school to adopt a child, confessed he was struggling with a lack of sleep due to the baby constantly waking in the night, a jury heard.

On April 6, he texted his sister, a baby sleep trainer: “He’s dead meat today. Didn’t sleep last night after 11.30. Up every, one and a half hours.”

Jurors heard once in the defendant’s care, Preston was taken to hospital three times – once with a fractured left elbow.

He was allegedly routinely ill-treated, sexually abused, physically assaulted and had indecent photos taken of him.

Just four months after he was adopted, the baby died after suffering a cardiac arrest.



Jurors heard a post mortem found multiple non-accidental, internal and external injuries.

Preston’s cause of death was given as an acute obstruction of his upper airway.

The court was told this was caused either a smothering with a hand or fabric or the insertion of an object into Preston’s mouth.

Varley denies murder, manslaughter, sexual assault of a child under 13, two counts of assault by penetration, grievous bodily harm, five counts of child cruelty and further counts of making, taking and distributing indecent images.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

McGowan-Fazakerley pleaded not guilty to causing and allowing the death of a child, three counts of child cruelty and sexual assault of a child under 13.



The trial continues.

News.title: Our baby died after nursery worker strapped her face down on bean bag… she told her to ‘stop whingeing’ as she lay dying
News.content:
WHEN Katie Meehan received a call from her baby daughter Genevieve’s nursery on her first proper day in their care, she could never have anticipated the unimaginable horror and heartbreak to follow.

The nine-month-old tot, affectionately known as Gigi, died at nursery in the most horrific circumstances – strapped face down to a bean bag and left for 90 minutes at nap time by callous manager Kate Roughley at now-closed Tiny Toes Nursery in Stockport.



For mum-of-three Katie, 41, and her barrister husband John, 40, putting their adored baby in nursery was not a decision they’d taken lightly – but never for one second did they think their daughter would come to any harm.

However, cruel worker Roughley swaddled Genevieve for her afternoon nap so tightly inside a blanket that she couldn’t move.

CCTV catches visibly-distressed Genevieve crying on several occasions, but her calls for help were ignored, and Roughley had also previously told her to “stop whingeing”.



In May 2024, she was sentenced to 14 years in prison for Genevieve’s death after being found guilty of manslaughter.

Katie says: “Listening to the details, it felt like Gigi died all over again, killed in front of me. To hear she’d been struggling for ninety minutes and was frightened – it plays on my mind every day.”

Harrowingly, Gigi died in May 2022 – the same year 14-month-old Noah Sibanda died at Fairytales Day Nursery in Dudley, West Midlands, “alone, scared and in pain” after staff at used “excessive” force to force him to nap.

Last month, nursery worker Kimberley Cookson was finally sentenced to three years and four months in prison for gross negligence manslaughter relating to Noah’s death.

Katie, who also has two other daughters, aged ten and three, says: “The thought of this happening to anybody else is unbearable, so to think another child could die like that in the same year is just heartbreaking.”



Similarly to Noah’s mum Masi, who said she felt guilty “knowing I handed him over to people who killed him”, Katie has also been plagued by regret for trusting a nursery to care for her cherished baby.

She says: “I felt very guilty because I’m Genevieve’s mum, and I didn’t know that was happening to her. It feels unbelievable that as she was dying, I was just sitting at home. She’d been verbally abused too, and I just didn’t know.”

In July 2021, Genevieve was born premature at thirty-four weeks, weighing 3lb 12oz, and had grown to be a happy, excitable baby who loved to dance.



The weekend before she died, Katie recalls with great fondness.

Katie says: “We just did simple things, but I just loved us being all together.

“Whenever she was happy, she’d bounce excitedly. She had been walking on my feet, and she’d started saying dada.

“She loved playing with all her toys, and she’d tried some new foods too, like summer fruit pudding. To this day, I still have some of her snacks in the cupboard.”

Gigi had visited the nursery on eight occasions, including short settling-in sessions, and the day she died, 9 May 2022, was her first full day.



Katie says: “I felt sad about missing out on time together.

“I was dreading it, so we’d pick her up early when we could.

“I said to John one day, ‘What if they’re not nice to her?’ and he said, ‘Of course they’ll be nice to her.’

“When sending your child to nursery, you assume as a parent that safety is a given.



“Never ever do you think they might not come home at the end of the day.”

Tiny Toes was temporary, as Katie had found another nursery close to her older daughter’s school and they were waiting for a place, but she knew it had a good reputation.

She says: “I would have loved to have stayed at home with my children, but I needed a nursery so I could provide for them, and I wanted the girls to know their mum worked hard.

“When choosing, we spoke to other parents. This nursery had been going for a long time, and I knew lots of people whose children had been there.

“They had people who’d worked there for over ten years, which I also thought must be a good thing.



“I looked at the Ofsted report, and they were rated ‘good’, and there was no record of any complaints.

“But we were later shocked to find out inspections only happen once every six years.

“This has recently been changed to four, but it’s still too infrequent when you’re dealing with babies.”



That Monday initially started out like any other day. Katie recalls: “That morning I said goodbye, and told her I loved her.

“She’d sat on the bed with me while I got ready, and I put suncream on her for the first time, which she found hilarious.

“That was another one of the reasons we couldn’t understand what happened to her. I kept saying to the doctor and police later that day – ‘but she’s fine, she’s so happy’.”

At first, when the nursery called Katie, who was at home working, she was told they’d gone to wake Genevieve up and she was limp and blue.

Katie says: “They said they were sorry and didn’t know what had happened. I was asking questions, but until I got to the hospital, I thought she’d be OK – there was no universe where I could imagine my baby would die.”



When Katie arrived however, in what can only be every parents’ worst nightmare, hospital staff were battling to resuscitate Genevieve.

She says: “They came over and asked to speak to us in another room, so I knew then she was gone.

“I couldn’t accept it. The desperation I felt that day has never left me.

“I didn’t want to leave her at the hospital, but as the hours passed, she didn’t seem like Genevieve anymore. It was physically painful.”



‘Something didn’t seem right’

In the days that followed, Katie struggled to comprehend what had happened.

She says: “We were told Genevieve was in a cot and she just coughed, and died.

“We didn’t know something sinister had happened, but we also couldn’t understand how Genevieve, at her age, would die of sudden infant death.

“I’d been hyper-aware of the dangers of sleep because she’d been premature, but I knew the risks decreased with age over six months.



“Something didn’t seem right, and we found out very quickly Genevieve had been placed to sleep on a beanbag when police viewed CCTV footage.”

A conviction in Genevieve’s case would never have happened without CCTV.

Which is why, as part of a campaign in Gigi’s name, Katie and John are pushing for CCTV to be mandatory in all nurseries, as well as better, safer sleep training to be provided to all workers, and more robust inspection policies.

In June 2022, Genevieve’s funeral was held. Katie says: “We didn’t go to a church, but we had a service and filled the venue with beautiful flowers, then we went and had spaghetti bolognese – Genevieve’s favourite food.

“We had to keep going for my oldest daughter, who was six. She still needed to go to school, so the focus became trying to protect her.”



Attending Roughley’s trial and sentencing two years later in May 2024, was agonising for Katie and John, who went every day in the hope for justice for their baby.

Katie says: “We believe she knew what she should be doing, and she knew that what she did was wrong.

“You give so much time and love to your children and they’re everything, so special. To think that somebody can just take that away – it’s so cruel.”

‘I can’t trust anybody’

Katie went on to find out she was pregnant with her youngest daughter, now three, a few months after Gigi’s death.

She says: “When I found out I felt like I was betraying Genevieve, but we had so much love to give.



“I knew I couldn’t bring Genevieve back, but I needed someone to care for, and I needed to have a baby in the family.

“That pregnancy was so hard. I had support from wonderful health visitors, but I constantly feared she was going to die.”

Now, Katie and John are making impressive progress in their campaign to improve nursery safety for others – but the damage and heartbreak caused to their family can never be undone.

Katie adds: “I’m so frightened of anything happening to my family, I spend the day constantly worrying.

“I haven’t used a nursery for my youngest, and I can’t trust anybody.



“For a long time, we kept Genevieve’s room as it was, but then I’d feel guilty that it would get dusty, so we all decided to decorate it together, with a woodland theme, as Genevieve has a wild flower garden.”

An inquest had been due to begin in June, but has been delayed after the coroner referred the case to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) after evidence indicated possible gross negligence manslaughter and corporate manslaughter.

It’s a move Katie has welcomed while she continues to focus on raising awareness around nursery safety in Gigi’s name, finally adding: “I want people to feel confident in asking questions. I don’t want people to experience this.

“Their child deserves to live and to thrive and to have everything. That’s what all children deserve.”

News.title: Teen apprentice left with horror burns after fireball explosion at work begged nurses to let him die
News.content:
WORKPLACE TRAGEDY Teen apprentice left with horror burns after fireball explosion at work begged nurses to let him die

A TEENAGE apprentice welder left with horrific burns after a fireball explosion at work has told how he begged nurses to let him die.

Dwayne Bell was just 17 years old when he was turned into a “human fireball” after a nightmare workplace accident at the steel yard where he was training.





As an apprentice welder at a steelworks in Wigan, Dwayne was asked to perform the routine task of burning rubbish.

But disaster struck when he added paint thinner to try and ignite some damp wood in the metal barrel.

He failed to notice sparks which had already caught under the wood, which caused the cylinder filled with paper and cardboard to explode with flames.

“I was standing in the middle of a massive flame. As soon as I felt the whoosh of heat I shut my eyes as I didn’t want to go blind,” he told Manchester Evening News.





“It was like a bomb exploding in my face.”

Dwayne, now aged 22, shared his story to raise awareness for other young trainees about the grave dangers they could face at work.

Pictures reveal the full extent of his devastating injuries, with burns covering eight per cent of his body.

His face and hands were completely scorched, left red and blistered with third degree burns which melted parts of his nose and ears.

Colleagues ran to his aide, putting out his flaming clothes which had caught ablaze.



In shock, he asked them to take a photo of his face, which was covered in feathers from his jacket, which had split open from the force of the blast.

Airlifted to hospital, his injuries were so severe that he was put in an induced coma for one week, waking up in “indescribable pain”.

“I looked at the nurses and I just begged them to let me die. I couldn’t see a future,” he painfully recalled.

Recovering at home after he was finally released from hospital, the young trainee described the pain as a “living nightmare”.

He suffered through three skin grafts over the next year, with his hands still badly damaged.



While he has returned to welding with another firm, his scarring limits how long he can work with the heat and vibration from power tools.

Now, he hopes his story could help other young apprentices in a similar position.

News.title: I was a mobster for 28 years & shot a man in the head before snitching, new life got me kicked off witness protection
News.content:
MAFIA enforcer Robert Borelli had to be approached with caution. He didn’t “value life” and he wasn’t slow to take offence.

Being given “bad quality cocaine” led the former New York drug dealer to shoot a man in the head, and he put anyone displaying disrespect “in their place.”





Over nearly 30 years in the mob, Borelli, now 71, was questioned about four murders. He did time for racketeering and worked for some of the Gambino family’s most feared men.

But the Wise Guy had two almost fatal weaknesses – women and drugs.

His “good life” ended after his inability to resist his own addictive substances left him homeless.

Then, having taken his life into his hands by informing on his former paymasters, Borelli risked his safety in the Witness Protection Program by revealing his identity to the woman he loved.

While many gangsters tend to glamourise their wealth and power, Borelli is a cautionary tale.

The reformed criminal now warns others about the dangers of working for the Mob.

Despite all the trappings of the life of a gangster, he was not a happy man.

Borelli tells The Sun: “What made me more dangerous than those people is I didn’t value my life and so people understood that if I didn’t value my own life I wasn’t going to value there’s either.





“I did have a reputation. A lot of people were afraid of me.”

Born into a respectable family struggling to make ends meet in East Brooklyn, Brownsville, Borelli looked longingly at the well dressed mobsters.

He recalls: “These guys down the block at the social club seemed to have it altogether.

“They dressed really nice, they had money in their pocket, they had cars, things that were really hard for people in my neighbourhood to have.”

By the time he was 14-years-old, Borelli was playing pool at one of the Mafia clubs and serving sandwiches during card games.

He continues: “If you’ve seen Goodfellas or something like it resembled how I grew up in my early teens.”

‘They knew if they mess with me the consequences could be extreme’

Soon, it turned violent.

Borelli admits: “Back in 1973 we had a fight outside a bar and somebody got killed and I was wanted for that murder.”

Being ‘respected’, was a key part of the gangster code and if they felt anyone was undermining their reputation it had to be sorted out.

Whether someone needed ‘putting straight’ or not, depended on the circumstances.



Unflinchingly, he says: “They knew if they mess with me the consequences could be extreme.

“That’s the kind of respect I got in the neighbourhood. I was given a lot of respect from the bosses, the way I handle myself.

“My friend Nicky Caruso’s father, when I walked into the club and he happened to be there, he would call me Quick Draw McGraw.

“That I thought was cute because he knew the type of guy I was. I carried a gun all the time and wouldn’t be afraid to use it.

“I think that was friendly I don’t think it was disrespectful, what was being said to me.

“And then there’s other times when people said something to me that degraded me a little bit, then I had to put them in their place.”

By the late 1970s, Borelli moved on from gambling to selling cocaine.

Unfortunately, he made the mistake of trying his own product far too often.



“I got involved with the drug business and eventually the drugs got involved with my business,” Borelli recalls, “and I was taking coke more and freebasing and using crack cocaine and before you know it, I was in bad shape getting hooked on cocaine.”

One time, after ‘freebasing’ cocaine to make it more potent, he started to believe a fellow user was withholding the best drugs.

Borelli admits: “I got really upset. I thought he was robbing me.”

Rather than acting immediately, he waited a few hours until he was in his ‘right mind’ and borrowed a gun to take revenge.

Fortunately, the weapon was faulty.

He explains: “I shot him in the head. What happened was the gun wasn’t really a stable gun so it broke in my hand.

“Then I guess the power of the bullet wasn’t strong enough and it got stuck in his forehead.

“From what I heard, when he ran out in the street he got hit by an ambulance that happened to be passing by and they took him to the hospital.”

‘Embarrassment to mobsters’

Gradually, the illegal substance got the better of him.

The ex-dealer recalls: “I lived a good life. I had a hotel room and there I was getting high, girls and stuff like that, but what happened was later on I couldn’t function without it.“



No matter how hard he tried, Borelli was unable to kick his drug habit, even when he became a dad.

“I was in a rehab cleaning up and my girlfriend was pregnant with my daughter at the time,” he says, “I wanted to clean up my act.”

Sobriety didn’t last for long and by the mid 1990s, his addiction was an “embarrassment” to his fellow mobsters so it was suggested that he go live with his mum in Florida.

A period of clean living was followed by more drugs, a failed rehab and his lowest ebb.

Borelli says: “It came to a point in 1996 when I was completely homeless living in the street in New York in Queens.

“Being homeless at the time I lost respect for myself and I know a lot of people lost respect for me.”

He got caught selling crack cocaine to an undercover officer and then was arrested for racketeering. The latter crime resulted in a two year-jail term.

During this time, Borelli decided to cooperate with the authorities, agreeing to give evidence against fellow Gambino gangster Anthony “Tony Pep” Trentacosta.

His mum did not approve of him turning against his colleagues and she died from lung cancer in April 1999 while he was in the Witness Protection Program.

Wistfully, he recalls: “My mom died when I was in the Witness Protection Program and nobody knew where I was.



“If they had to get in touch with me, they had to go through the Marshalls. I didn’t know that my mom passed away until three days after she passed away.”

‘Thrown out of the witness protection programme’

It was during his time in the protection program that Borelli found God, studying religion at the Christ For The Nations ministry in Texas.

He also met a woman, who he wanted to commit to. Perhaps, understandably he felt she should know that he was a reformed gangster whose life was at risk.

Borelli says: “The government didn’t want me to tell this girl that I was in the Witness Protection Program.

“I was going to ask her to marry me then I just said there’s no way that I can’t tell her something like that and ask her to marry me.

“Because she was from New York and they felt it would put my security at risk. I told her and they threw me out of the program.”

These days he is a different person in many ways. Borelli is not his real name and he has turned his back on crime and drugs.

Borelli has written a book and has a YouTube channel, where he talks about going from Mafia to ministry.

He says: “These documentaries that I did were about bringing the message of hope for the people who felt they were hopeless.

“I always preach that it’s never too late for a new beginning in life no matter where you’re stuck – you’re not stuck, you don’t have to stay stuck there.



“I’m very peaceful I love serving God.”

Watch Robert Borelli’s YouTube channel @RobertBorelliStories

News.title: Parents feel loneliest five months after birth as support drops and reality hits
News.content:
BABY BLUES Parents feel loneliest five months after birth as support drops and reality hits

PARENTS feel most lonely five months after having a baby – when the reality of having a newborn kicks in and friends and family are less available.

A poll of 1,000 parents with a child aged under five found more than half (55 per cent) have experienced loneliness since having their baby.



Despite the first few months being filled with excitement (56 per cent), visits from family and friends (48 per cent) and adrenaline (37 per cent), the sense of support didn’t always last.

For a third (34 per cent), loneliness was driven by the reality of life with a newborn setting in, as well as a growing sense that their priorities no longer aligned with those of their friends (35 per cent).



More than half of mums (56 per cent) and nearly a third (31 per cent) of dads said they felt lonely even when they were with their baby.

Worryingly, three quarters (76 per cent) admitted they hid how they were feeling from others.

The study was commissioned by Aldi, which has collaborated with perinatal mental health charity, PANDAS Foundation, to raise awareness of, and reduce stigma around, the wellbeing of new parents for Maternal Mental Health Week (4th –10th May).

The research also found 58 per cent would run errands simply for the chance to interact with others – even when they didn’t need anything.

Supermarkets (67 per cent), parks (42 per cent) and cafés (42 per cent) were among the most common places where parents interacted with others, with nearly half (47 per cent) feeling relieved when a stranger spoke to them.

Julie Ashfield, chief commercial officer at Aldi UK, said: “Support is often strongest in those early weeks of parenthood – but our research shows it’s the months that follow where many parents can feel most alone.

“That’s why it’s so important we keep checking in, long after the initial excitement has passed.”

Sally Bunkham, for the mental health charity, said: “Once your baby arrives, everything changes.



“It can feel overwhelming in ways many parents don’t expect, even during what’s meant to be one of the happiest times.

“Early interventional support is so important, making sure parents feel seen, supported, and not alone from the very beginning.”

The research also found just a few months into parenthood, 51 per cent experienced a slump in their mood, with many saying they felt anxious about what the next phase would bring.

Parents said they saw fewer people once their partner returned to work (61 per cent), with 57 per cent reporting they had the most interaction with others in the earliest weeks after their baby was born.

Of those, 39 per cent said visits and conversations slowed down after the first few months, while exactly a quarter admitted they simply didn’t have the energy to socialise.



During this time, mums spent an average of seven hours a day alone with their baby, while dads experienced this for four hours.

Despite a clear feeling of loneliness, the top emotion when first having their child was excitement, according to 72 per cent of those polled via OnePoll.

Others were overwhelmed (58 per cent) and exhausted (44 per cent) while also being grateful (57 per cent).

Dr Caroline Boyd, clinical psychologist, author and PANDAS ambassador, said: “These findings reflect a common but often hidden experience of early parenthood – a period where loneliness can intensify as support drops away and parents are still adjusting to their new identity.

“In the context of this profound transition, feeling connected to trusted others is not a luxury but essential, particularly in a culture that places pressure on parents to cope alone.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“This is why initiatives like our partnership with Aldi are so important in raising awareness and encouraging parents to seek out spaces where they feel safe enough to share how they’re really feeling.”

The supermarket is donating £20,000 from proceeds of Mamia baby wipe sales, which have QR codes to scan for support on packs, to PANDAS Foundation during Maternal Mental Health Awareness Week.

News.title: Where is my polling station? How to find your place to vote in 2026 local elections and what time polls open
News.content:
MILLIONS of voters will head to the polls for local elections in early May, with more than 5,000 council seats being contested.

Here’s everything you need to know about finding your local polling station and what time the doors open and close, so you can have your say.





How do I find my polling station?

Polling stations are assigned based on where you live, with the address printed on the poll card that drops through your letterbox a few weeks before election day.

So the quickest way to track yours down is to check your poll card, which is sent out by your local council.

The card lists the address of the polling station you have been allocated, along with the date of the election and your ward name.

It’s important to remember that you can only vote at the polling station shown on your card – even if there is one closer to home, you will not be allowed to use it.

If you don’t have your card to hand, you can find out where to vote by entering your postcode on the Electoral Commission’s online tool.

It tells you where your polling station is, who is standing, and who to contact if you need help.

What time do polling stations open?

Polling stations across England will be open from 7am to 10pm on Thursday, May 7, 2026.

You can pop in to vote at any time during that 15-hour window.



If you are already inside the polling station, or even waiting in the queue outside when the doors close at 10pm, staff are required to let you cast your vote.

Most polling stations are set up in public buildings like schools, community centres, libraries or church halls.

To vote in person you will need to bring an accepted form of photo ID to vote, following changes to the law in 2023.

That includes a a UK passport, photocard driving licence, blue badge, and an older person’s bus pass, among others.

You also need to be registered to vote at your current address.



If you don’t have one of the accepted IDs, it is possible to apply for a free Voter Authority Certificate, but the deadline – 5pm on Tuesday, April 28 – has now passed.

The registration deadline to vote in the local elections – 11.59pm on Monday, April 20 – has also now passed.

What if I’ve lost my poll card?

You don’t actually need your poll card to vote.

As long as you are on the electoral register and bring an accepted form of photo ID, you will still be allowed to cast your ballot.

If you would like a replacement card or want to check your polling station details, you can contact your local council’s electoral services team.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Their contact details are listed on the Electoral Commission website by postcode, which is the same link as above.

If you can’t get to the polling station on the day, it is possible apply for a postal or proxy vote, but the April 21 deadline has now passed.

News.title: Major update on condition of Brit doctor rescued from Hantavirus cruise ship
News.content:
Major update on condition of Brit doctor rescued from Hantavirus cruise ship

It is believed Hantavirus was brought onto MV Hondius, by a Dutch couple who had gone birdwatching at a landfill site in Ushuaia, Argentina, before boarding the ship

View 6 Images Three people, one of whom pictured, were medically evacuated from the marooned cruise ship

A British doctor evacuated from the cruise ship marooned after a deadly Hantavirus outbreak struck is 'stable' but in a “serious condition”.

‌



It is feared the virus, which has killed three passengers, was brought onto the ship by a Dutch couple who had gone on a bird watching trip. The bird loving couple were the first to report symptoms four days after the cruise began and both later died.

‌



The 70-year-old man and his 69-year-old wife had been travelling in Argentina before their dream trip and had gone bird watching in the coastal city of Ushuaia, where the boat was docked.

‌



Argentine officials investigating the origins of the hantavirus outbreak on the cruise ship told AP their Government’s leading hypothesis is that a Dutch couple contracted the virus during a bird-watching outing in the city before boarding. They said the couple visited a landfill during the bird-watching tour where they may have been exposed to rodents carrying the infection.

Previously authorities said that Ushuaia and the surrounding province of Tierra del Fuego had never recorded a case of the hantavirus which was more prevalent in rural areas inland.

View 6 Images Three people were taken off the ship, including two crew members (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Hantavirus outbreak on cruise may be linked to couple's trip to landfill site READ MORE :

Some 19 British nationals were listed as passengers on the ship, which was sailing from Argentina to Cape Verde, with four British crew members.

Eight people on the ship are believed to have been exposed to the virus, three have died, and three are in a serious condition, another is showing no symptoms and one man tested positive for the virus after leaving the ship. In total three have been confirmed as having the virus after tests, including the 69-year-old British passenger who is still in intensive care in Johannesburg.

On Wednesday three people were medically evacuated from the ship, including the 56 year old British doctor who is said to be serious but ‘stable’ and a Dutch crew member, aged 41. They were both flown to a Netherlands medical facility. A German national, aged 65, had no symptoms but was also evacuated as they had been travelling with the man who died, will return to Germany.

‌



Before disaster struck, passengers described their five week voyage from Argentina to Cape Verde as “unreal” filming rare dolphins and birds, then thrilled to finally set foot on the remotest inhabited island in the world, Tristan Da Cunha.

View 6 Images Ruhi Cenet, a filmmaker, criticises the ship's management (Image: ruhicenet/Instagram)

Ruhi Cenet, a filmmaker, shared a video on Instagram showing a senior crew member announcing the first death and criticised the vessel’s management for not locking them down sooner.

‌



His film shows the Captain speaking to passengers in the ship’s lounge, using a microphone. He announces: ‘This is my sad duty to inform you that one of our passengers sadly passed away last night…it was due to natural causes I believe…I’m told by the doctor they are not infectious and the ship is safe when it comes to that.”

View 6 Images The Captain talks about his sadness and reassures passengers they do not think it is 'infectious' (Image: ruhicenet/Instagram)

Ruhi then described how his journey went wrong and says in his video: “When one of the passengers died during a month-long journey on an expedition vessel, I honestly thought it was because of the rough ocean conditions.

‌



“But it turns out the situation was much worse than we were told. I got off the ship on Day 24 but this vessel called MV Hondius continued towards its final destination for another 11 days.

“Just after one day I left the ship, the wife of the person who had died also passed away. And after a third person died it became clear that there was Hantavirus on board, a virus transmitted by rodents with no treatment available.

“It was only later understood that the first person who had died, died actually because of this virus. Now the ship’s only doctor is also fighting for his life.”

‌



He added: “All the passengers are stuck in an unknown quarantine situation…”

"I wish the vessel’s management had taken this problem more seriously from the very first death; they should have thought that it might be a contagious disease. People who may have been carrying the virus should have been quarantined. But everyone was still together, meals were still eaten together and group activities continued.”

He said blood tests should have been taken before such a long journey started.

‌



View 6 Images Medics in hazmat suits have been coming and going trying with the help of a pilot ship to treat the stricken passengers including a British doctor (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

But Oceanwide Expeditions, the cruise operators, said they were aware of the video circulating on social media and wanted to point out the announcement to guests was made on April 12th, the day after a Dutch national died.

They said; “This onboard announcement was made on 12 April 2026. On this date, the cause of death of this individual was unknown. No other symptomatic individuals were present on board.

‌



“At the time of the announcement, no evidence of a virus or contagion was present on the vessel. The case was believed to be isolated following medical review.

“Proper procedure was followed in informing all guests and crew aboard m/v Hondius. Health and safety and maritime standards regarding the proper management and reporting of a death while at sea were followed."

Jake Rosmarin, who earlier posted a tearful video about being stranded on the ship, later posted a picture of himself smiling adding: "Spirits are still high…we are being well fed and cared for.”

‌



Others had posted online about their frustration a dead body and sick crew members were not being allowed off the ship which was due to disembark on Monday in Cape Verde.

It took at least three days for the doctor to be medically evacuated and taken to a specialist aircraft which had been sent from the Netherlands to collect him.

He was evacuated alongside another Dutch crew member who was sick and a German passenger, who was connected to the man who died on May 2nd.

‌



Hantavirus: British crew member needs ‘urgent’ care after suspected outbreak on cruise ship

The first passenger to die, a Dutch man aged 70, passed away on April 11th as the ship arrived in St Helena. His wife, aged 69, died after being flown to South Africa. It is believed she was taken off a connecting flight to the Netherlands because of her medical condition.

South African authorities are now tracing 90 people on her flight. Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi said: “Preliminary tests show that it is indeed the Andes strain. And it turns out to be the only one of the 38 known strains that can be transmitted from person to person. But as we said, and we want to reiterate, this type of transmission is very rare and only occurs due to very close contact between people .”

‌



Those infected suffered symptoms including fever and gastrointestinal illness to pneumonia, respiratory failure, and shock.

Swiss authorities have confirmed that a case of Hantavirus had been identified in a passenger who'd left the cruise ship and had responded to an alert and presented himself to a hospital in Zurich.

WHO director Tedros Ghebreyesus said: "At this stage, the overall public health risk remains low."

‌



Oceanwide Expeditions revealed two infectious disease physicians from the Netherlands, were joining the ship before it was due to leave for a three day journey from Cape Verde to the Canary Islands.

But it was up in the air if they would be allowed to dock there.

Spain’s health ministry said it would receive the ship in Tenerife after a request from the WHO and the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control.

‌



But the Canary Islands regional president, Fernando Clavijo, said he worried about the risk to the population and demanded a meeting with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

View 6 Images The cruise ship pictured anchored at a port in Praia, Cape Verde (Image: AP)

The plan is that once in Tenerife, all non-Spanish passengers will be repatriated to their countries while the Spanish passengers will be taken to a military hospital in Madrid for quarantine.

‌



The ship is expected at Granadilla where there will be a system for assessing the passengers and progressing their repatriation back to countries of origin, they said.

Oceanwide Expeditions said: “We can confirm that the three individuals previously indicated as awaiting medical transfer have been successfully disembarked from m/v Hondius...Two of the individuals remain in a serious condition. The third, while currently asymptomatic, was closely associated with the individual who passed away on board on 2 May 2026. The two symptomatic individuals have not tested positive for hantavirus at this time.”

Passengers on the ship are being urged to stay in their cabins and have been keeping themselves busy by reading, watching movies and having hot drinks.

‌



The World Health Organisation’s top epidemic expert Maria Van Kerkhove said. “This is not the next Covid, but it is a serious infectious disease. Most people will never be exposed to this.”

On Wednesday, Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper said: "The Foreign Office is working urgently to support the UKHSA's (UK Health Security Agency's) work overseas and to make sure British nationals on the MV Hondius can all get safely home with proper protection for public health.

"Foreign Office consular staff are in direct contact with British nationals onboard the ship and stand ready to provide further assistance to any British national in need of support overseas 24/7 - our crisis response centre has been operating for the last few days to provide support.

Article continues below

"Ministers are in close touch with our Dutch and Spanish counterparts and we have been working with other countries to facilitate the medical evacuations, to support our overseas territories and to get British nationals home safely as quickly as possible."

News.title: Jet carrying sick airlifted from virus-ravaged cruise turned away from airport
News.content:
Jet carrying sick airlifted from virus-ravaged cruise turned away from airport

The emergency evacuation flight carrying two seriously ill people had been scheduled to refuel in Marrakech, Morocco - but the landing was refused

View Image The Learjet 45 was refused permission to land to refuel (Image: AP)

A medical plane carrying two people evacuated from the virus-ravaged cruise liner MV Hondius was forced to make an unscheduled stop this afternoon after being refused permission to land in Morocco.

‌



The Learjet 45 had been scheduled to refuel in Marrakech after health personnel removed the pair in hazmat suits on stretchers from the boat off the Cape Verde coast. But the emergency flight ended up having to reroute to Gando Air Base, a Spanish Air Force hub on the east coast of Gran Canaria, after Moroccan air traffic control refused the landing request.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Article continues below

The flight was due to leave again for its final destination of Holland around 5.40pm local time today. It was not immediately clear if the patient on board was the seriously-ill British doctor evacuated earlier today.

News.title: Snooker’s ultimate rich list with new champion Wu Yize only just inside wealthiest top 50
News.content:
Snooker’s ultimate rich list with new champion Wu Yize only just inside wealthiest top 50

New world champion Wu Yize ranks far behind some of snooker's other top names

View 2 Images Wu Yize recently won the World Snooker Championship (Image: George Wood, Getty Images)

New world champion Wu Yize is not among the leading names in snooker's all-time prize money list. The 22-year-old triumphed over Shaun Murphy in the recent World Snooker Championship final and received £500,000 for his efforts.

‌



Wu produced a dramatic 18-17 win at the Crucible to claim the sport's most prestigious prize. However, the rising star remains 47th in the all-time rich list, while two household names fail to crack the top five.

‌



Snooker icons Stephen Hendry and Steve Davis won a combined 13 world titles during their careers, but neither occupies a top-five place. Davis reigned supreme at the Crucible during the 1980s, winning six world championships, and ended his career with 28 ranking titles.

‌



The 68-year-old hung up his cue in 2016, with CueTracker recording his total prize money at £5.6million, putting him 10th on the all-time list, four spots beneath Hendry. The Scotsman secured seven world titles, a record he shares with Ronnie O'Sullivan, but his £8.8m in prize money sees him sit sixth.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

CueTracker states that O'Sullivan is the sport's highest earner of all-time. 'The Rocket', who has won 41 ranking events, has collected £15.1m in prize money, which is £4m ahead of his closest challenger.

‌



Ronnie O'Sullivan returns to Crucible immediately after Wu Yize wins World Snooker Championship READ MORE :

Shaun Murphy faces double blow after losing World Snooker Championship final to Wu Yize READ MORE :

Despite O'Sullivan topping the rich list, numerous other players have built substantial fortunes through the sport. Fellow Class of '92 legend John Higgins occupies second spot as the 50-year-old has gathered a substantial £11.1m in prize money.

Current world No.1 Judd Trump sits in fourth position with £10m, putting him ahead of four-time world champion Mark Selby, who has accumulated £9.2m in prize money. Mark Williams ensures all three members of the legendary Class of '92 feature in the top five after amassing £9m throughout his career.

While Hendry comes up marginally short of Williams' figure, his prize money haul places him in front of Neil Robertson, who has banked £8.2m. Meanwhile, recent world championship runner-up Shaun Murphy occupies eighth spot with £7.1m followed by Mark Allen's £6.1m in prize money.

‌



View 2 Images Ronnie O'Sullivan leads snooker's all-time prize money list (Image: Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images)

Outside of the top 10, notable names include 2024 world champion Kyren Wilson in 12th with £5.2m, followed by snooker icon Jimmy White on £4.9m. Ali Carter (16th, £4m), Ken Doherty (17th, £3.8m) and Peter Ebdon (19th, £3.6m) also rank within the top 20. The 2025 World Snooker Championship winner Zhao Xintong is 28th with £2.3m.

Chinese star Wu's recent winnings have propelled him up to 47th on the list, narrowly above Dennis Taylor, with his career earnings now standing at £1.4m. Wu's compatriot Ding Junhui sits 11th with an impressive £5.4m.

‌



O'Sullivan has a chance to increase his advantage on the all-time list as he gets ready to compete in the World Seniors Championship. 'The Rocket' is due to make his tournament debut on Friday, with the event offering a £30,000 top prize.
